कथन V सही है क्योंकि hnRNA के 5'-छोर पर मेथिल ग्वानोसिन ट्राइफॉस्फेट का जुड़ना कैपिंग कहलाता है, जो इसे न्यूक्लियेज से सुरक्षित रखता है।

चरण 2: सही संयोजन का चयन
कथन I, II और V सही हैं, जबकि कथन III और IV गलत हैं।

अंतिम उत्तर:
केवल कथन I, II और V सही हैं।

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MULTISTATEMENT_Q05 - Salient features of genetic code, point mutations, and tRNA structure

questiontext.text:
Consider the following five statements regarding the genetic code, gene mutations, and the tRNA adapter molecule:

Statement I: Among the 64 possible triplet codons, 61 codons specify 20 amino acids, while three codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) do not code for any amino acid and function as stop signals.

Statement II: The genetic code is degenerate because multiple distinct codons can code for the same specific amino acid.

Statement III: The genetic code is non-universal without exception, differing completely between bacterial, plant, animal, and human nuclear genes.

Statement IV: A point mutation resulting from a single base substitution converting the GAG codon to GUG in the β-globin gene leads to the substitution of glutamic acid by valine, causing sickle-cell anemia.

Statement V: In two dimensions, the secondary structure of tRNA resembles a cloverleaf, whereas its actual tertiary compact structure resembles an inverted L shape.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

आनुवंशिक कूट (जेनेटिक कोड), जीन उत्परिवर्तन तथा tRNA अनुकूलक अणु के संबंध में निम्नलिखित पांच कथनों पर विचार कीजिए:

कथन I: कुल 64 संभावित त्रिक प्रकूटों में से 61 प्रकूट 20 अमीनो अम्लों का कूटलेखन करते हैं, जबकि तीन प्रकूट (UAA, UAG, UGA) किसी भी अमीनो अम्ल का कूटलेखन नहीं करते और रोध प्रकूट के रूप में कार्य करते हैं।

कथन II: आनुवंशिक कूट अपह्रसित (अपभ्रष्ट) होता है क्योंकि एक ही विशिष्ट अमीनो अम्ल एक से अधिक प्रकूटों द्वारा कोडित हो सकता है।

कथन III: आनुवंशिक कूट बिना किसी अपवाद के असा सार्वभौमिक (गैर-सार्वत्रिक) होता है, जो जीवाणु, पादप, जंतु और मानव के केंद्रकीय जीनों में पूरी तरह भिन्न होता है।

कथन IV: β-ग्लोबिन जीन में एकल क्षार प्रतिस्थापन द्वारा GAG प्रकूट के GUG में बदलने से ग्लूटामिक अम्ल का स्थान वैलीन ले लेता है, जिससे दात्र कोशिका अरक्तता (सिकल-सेल एनीमिया) रोग होता है।

कथन V: द्विविमीय रूप में tRNA की द्वितीयक संरचना तिपतिया घास की पत्ती (क्लोवर-लीफ) जैसी दिखती है, जबकि इसकी वास्तविक त्रिविमीय संहत संरचना उल्टे L (इन्वर्टेड L) के आकार की होती है।

उपर्युक्त कथनों में से कौन-से सही हैं?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of individual statements
Statement I is correct because 61 codons assign 20 standard amino acids, while UAA (ochre), UAG (amber), and UGA (opal) do not recruit aminoacyl-tRNAs and serve as translation termination codons.
Statement II is correct because degeneracy of the genetic code signifies that most amino acids (except methionine and tryptophan) are specified by more than one codon.
Statement III is incorrect because the genetic code is nearly universal across all living forms; for instance, UUU codes for phenylalanine from bacteria to humans, with only minor differences documented in mitochondrial codons and certain protozoans.
Statement IV is correct because in sickle-cell anemia, a transversion mutation (A → T) at the 6th codon of the β-globin gene alters GAG (coding for glutamic acid) to GUG (coding for valine).
Statement V is correct because tRNA folds into a cloverleaf secondary structure due to internal base pairing, but X-ray crystallography reveals an actual compact inverted-L shaped 3D conformation.

Step 2: Selection of the correct combination
Statements I, II, IV, and V are correct, while Statement III is incorrect.

Final Answer:
Statements I, II, IV and V only.

चरण 1: व्यक्तिगत कथनों का मूल्यांकन
कथन I सही है क्योंकि 61 प्रकूट 20 अमीनो अम्लों का कूटलेखन करते हैं, जबकि UAA, UAG, और UGA किसी अमीनो अम्ल को कोड नहीं करते और प्रोटीन संश्लेषण समापन संकेत देते हैं।
कथन II सही है क्योंकि आनुवंशिक कूट की अपभ्रष्टता (डीजनरेसी) का अर्थ है कि अधिकांश अमीनो अम्ल एक से अधिक प्रकूटों द्वारा कोडित होते हैं।
कथन III गलत है क्योंकि आनुवंशिक कूट लगभग सार्वभौमिक (यूनिवर्सल) होता है; उदाहरण के लिए, UUU जीवाणु से लेकर मनुष्य तक फेनिलअलैनिन को ही कोड करता है (केवल माइटोकॉन्ड्रियल और कुछ प्रोटोजोआ में सूक्ष्म अपवाद हैं)।
कथन IV सही है क्योंकि सिकल-सेल एनीमिया में β-ग्लोबिन श्रृंखला के छठे प्रकूट में एकल क्षार प्रतिस्थापन GAG को GUG में बदल देता है, जिससे ग्लूटामिक अम्ल का स्थान वैलीन ले लेता है।
कथन V सही है क्योंकि tRNA की द्वितीयक संरचना क्लोवर-लीफ जैसी होती है, परंतु इसका वास्तविक त्रिविमीय संहत रूप उल्टे 'L' के आकार का होता है।

चरण 2: सही संयोजन का चयन
कथन I, II, IV और V सही हैं, जबकि कथन III गलत है।

अंतिम उत्तर:
केवल कथन I, II, IV और V सही हैं।

answer.text: Statements I, II, IV and V only
Statements II, III, IV and V only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MULTISTATEMENT_Q06 - Gene regulation by lac operon and major findings of Human Genome Project

questiontext.text:
Consider the following five statements regarding the regulation of gene expression in the lac operon and the landmark findings of the Human Genome Project (HGP):

Statement I: In the lac operon, the repressor protein constitutively synthesized by the i gene binds specifically to the operator region to prevent RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes.

Statement II: Lactose or allolactose acts as an inducer by interacting with the repressor protein, inactivating it and allowing RNA polymerase access to the promoter.

Statement III: The three structural genes of the lac operon—z, y, and a—encode β-galactosidase, permease, and transacetylase, respectively.

Statement IV: Major findings of the Human Genome Project demonstrated that the human genome contains more than 100,000 protein-coding genes, with chromosome Y possessing the greatest number of genes.

Statement V: According to the Human Genome Project, the total human genome contains approximately 3.1647 billion nucleotide base pairs, and less than 2 percent of the genome encodes proteins.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

lac प्रचालेक (लैक ओपेरॉन) में जीन अभिव्यक्ति के नियमन तथा मानव जीनोम परियोजना (HGP) की प्रमुख खोजों के संबंध में निम्नलिखित पांच कथनों पर विचार कीजिए:

कथन I: lac प्रचालेक में, i जीन द्वारा निरंतर संश्लेषित दमनकारी प्रोटीन विशेष रूप से प्रचालक (ऑपरेटर) स्थल से जुड़कर RNA पॉलीमरेज को संरचनात्मक जीनों के अनुलेखन से रोकता है।

कथन II: लैक्टोज अथवा एलोलैक्टोज प्रेरक के रूप में दमनकारी से जुड़कर उसे निष्क्रिय कर देता है, जिससे RNA पॉलीमरेज उन्नायक (प्रमोटर) से जुड़कर अनुलेखन कर पाता है।

कथन III: lac प्रचालेक के तीन संरचनात्मक जीन—z, y, और a—क्रमशः β-गैलेक्टोसिडेज, परमिएज, तथा ट्रांसएसिटिलेज का कूटलेखन करते हैं।

कथन IV: मानव जीनोम परियोजना की मुख्य खोजों ने दर्शाया कि मानव जीनोम में 1,00,000 से अधिक प्रोटीन-कोडिंग जीन होते हैं, जिनमें Y गुणसूत्र पर सर्वाधिक जीन उपस्थित होते हैं।

कथन V: मानव जीनोम परियोजना के अनुसार, कुल मानव जीनोम में लगभग 3.1647 अरब न्यूक्लियोटाइड क्षार युग्म होते हैं, और जीनोम का 2 प्रतिशत से भी कम भाग प्रोटीन का कूटलेखन करता है।

उपर्युक्त कथनों में से कौन-से सही हैं?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of individual statements
Statement I is correct because the i gene produces the repressor constitutively, which binds to the operator gene (o) blocking transcription of downstream structural genes in the absence of inducer.
Statement II is correct because the inducer (lactose/allolactose) binds to the repressor protein, causing conformational change and detachment from the operator, allowing RNA polymerase to proceed.
Statement III is correct because the polycistronic structural genes transcribe enzymes for lactose metabolism: z codes for β-galactosidase, y codes for permease, and a codes for transacetylase.
Statement IV is incorrect because HGP revealed that the human genome contains approximately 20,000–25,000 (roughly 30,000) protein-coding genes, far fewer than earlier estimates of 80,000–140,000; moreover, chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and chromosome Y has the fewest (231).
Statement V is correct because the human genome sequence consists of 3164.7 million (3.1647 billion) nucleotide base pairs, with less than 2% of the genome coding for functional proteins.

Step 2: Selection of the correct combination
Statements I, II, III, and V are correct, while Statement IV is incorrect.

Final Answer:
Statements I, II, III and V only.

चरण 1: व्यक्तिगत कथनों का मूल्यांकन
कथन I सही है क्योंकि i जीन द्वारा निर्मित दमनकारी प्रोटीन प्रचालक (ऑपरेटर) से जुड़कर RNA पॉलीमरेज के मार्ग को अवरुद्ध करता है।
कथन II सही है क्योंकि प्रेरक (लैक्टोज/एलोलैक्टोज) दमनकारी से जुड़कर उसे निष्क्रिय कर देता है, जिससे प्रचालेक का वि-दमन (derepression) हो जाता है।
कथन III सही है क्योंकि z जीन β-गैलेक्टोसिडेज, y जीन परमिएज, और a जीन ट्रांसएसिटिलेज को कूटबद्ध करते हैं।
कथन IV गलत है क्योंकि मानव जीनोम परियोजना ने स्थापित किया कि मानव जीनोम में केवल लगभग 30,000 जीन होते हैं (1,00,000 से अधिक नहीं); तथा गुणसूत्र 1 पर सर्वाधिक जीन (2968) और Y गुणसूत्र पर सबसे कम जीन (231) होते हैं।
कथन V सही है क्योंकि मानव जीनोम में 3164.7 मिलियन (लगभग 3.1647 अरब) क्षार युग्म पाए जाते हैं तथा 2 प्रतिशत से कम जीनोम प्रोटीन का कूटलेखन करता है।

चरण 2: सही संयोजन का चयन
कथन I, II, III और V सही हैं, जबकि कथन IV गलत है।

अंतिम उत्तर:
केवल कथन I, II, III और V सही हैं।

answer.text: Statements I, II, III and V only
Statements I, III, IV and V only

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q01 - Match organism with genomic base pair content

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Organism) List-II (Genetic Content)
A. \(\phi \times 174\) bacteriophage I. \(4.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\)
B. Bacteriophage lambda II. \(5386\text{ nucleotides}\)
C. Escherichia coli III. \(3.3 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\)
D. Human haploid genome IV. \(48502\text{ bp}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The task requires matching distinct organisms with their characteristic DNA lengths as defined by the number of nucleotides or base pairs.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Values
The length of DNA is defined by the number of nucleotides or base pairs characteristic of each organism. Specifically:
- Bacteriophage \(\phi \times 174\) has a single-stranded circular DNA genome containing \(5386\text{ nucleotides}\).
- Bacteriophage lambda has a double-stranded linear genome of \(48502\text{ base pairs}\) (\(\text{bp}\)).
- The bacterium Escherichia coli contains \(4.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\).
- The haploid genome of Homo sapiens contains \(3.3 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\) (whereas the diploid content is \(6.6 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\)).

Step 3: Pairing Identification
- \(\phi \times 174\) bacteriophage associates with \(5386\text{ nucleotides}\).
- Bacteriophage lambda associates with \(48502\text{ bp}\).
- Escherichia coli associates with \(4.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\).
- Human haploid genome associates with \(3.3 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
All base pair and nucleotide quantities align precisely with the established molecular values for these model organisms.
Final Answer: The correct matching is \(\phi \times 174\) bacteriophage with \(5386\text{ nucleotides}\); Bacteriophage lambda with \(48502\text{ bp}\); Escherichia coli with \(4.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\); and Human haploid genome with \(3.3 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q02 - Match scientist with historical molecular discovery

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Scientist) List-II (Contribution)
A. Friedrich Meischer I. X-ray diffraction data of DNA
B. James Watson and Francis Crick II. First identified DNA as an acidic substance called Nuclein
C. Erwin Chargaff III. Proposed the Double Helix model of DNA
D. Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin IV. Base ratio equality between Adenine-Thymine and Guanine-Cytosine

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The problem requires matching prominent historical researchers in molecular genetics with their direct contributions to the discovery and structural elucidation of DNA.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Discoveries
- Friedrich Meischer (1869) was the first to identify DNA as an acidic substance located inside cell nuclei and termed it 'Nuclein'.
- James Watson and Francis Crick (1953) formulated and proposed the famous Double Helix structural model for DNA.
- Erwin Chargaff observed that in double-stranded DNA, the ratios between Adenine and Thymine, as well as Guanine and Cytosine, remain constant and equal to one (\(A/T = 1\) and \(G/C = 1\)).
- Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin generated crucial X-ray diffraction photographic data that provided structural measurements for Watson and Crick's model.

Step 3: Pairing Identification
- Friedrich Meischer associates with first identifying DNA as an acidic substance called Nuclein.
- James Watson and Francis Crick associate with proposing the Double Helix model of DNA.
- Erwin Chargaff associates with base ratio equality between Adenine-Thymine and Guanine-Cytosine.
- Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin associate with X-ray diffraction data of DNA.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Each historical milestone correctly matches the scientist who performed the work.
Final Answer: The correct matching is Friedrich Meischer with First identified DNA as an acidic substance called Nuclein; James Watson and Francis Crick with Proposed the Double Helix model of DNA; Erwin Chargaff with Base ratio equality between Adenine-Thymine and Guanine-Cytosine; and Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin with X-ray diffraction data of DNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q03 - Match classic genetic experiments with methodologies

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Experimenter) List-II (Experimental Setup / Discovery)
A. Frederick Griffith I. Semiconservative replication proof using \(^{15}\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\) and CsCl gradient
B. Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, Maclyn McCarty II. Unequivocal proof of DNA as genetic material using \(^{32}\text{P}\) and \(^{35}\text{S}\)
C. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase III. Transformation principle demonstrated in Streptococcus pneumoniae
D. Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl IV. Biochemical proof that DNase inhibits transformation whereas proteases do not

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Match landmark biological experiments with their exact experimental design and conclusions.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Experiments
- Frederick Griffith (1928) injected mice with combinations of heat-killed virulent S strain and live non-virulent R strain of Streptococcus pneumoniae, discovering the phenomenon of transformation.
- Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty (1933-44) purified biochemicals from heat-killed S cells and established that only digestion with DNase inhibited transformation, proving that DNA was the transforming substance.
- Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952) employed radioactive bacteriophages labeled with phosphorus-32 (labeling DNA) and sulfur-35 (labeling protein coat) to unequivocally prove that DNA enters the bacterium and serves as the genetic material.
- Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl (1958) grew E. coli in heavy nitrogen isotope (\(^{15}\text{N}\)) followed by \(^{14}\text{N}\), using CsCl density gradient centrifugation to demonstrate semiconservative replication of DNA.

Step 3: Pairing Identification
- Frederick Griffith associates with transformation principle demonstrated in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
- Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, Maclyn McCarty associate with biochemical proof that DNase inhibits transformation whereas proteases do not.
- Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase associate with unequivocal proof of DNA as genetic material using \(^{32}\text{P}\) and \(^{35}\text{S}\).
- Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl associate with semiconservative replication proof using \(^{15}\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\) and CsCl gradient.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
All methodology pairs align precisely with standard experimental accounts.
Final Answer: The correct matching is Frederick Griffith with Transformation principle demonstrated in Streptococcus pneumoniae; Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, Maclyn McCarty with Biochemical proof that DNase inhibits transformation whereas proteases do not; Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase with Unequivocal proof of DNA as genetic material using \(^{32}\text{P}\) and \(^{35}\text{S}\); and Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl with Semiconservative replication proof using \(^{15}\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\) and CsCl gradient.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q04 - Match replication machinery components with specific roles

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Replication Component) List-II (Function / Characteristic)
A. DNA-dependent DNA polymerase I. Joins discontinuously synthesised fragments
B. Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates II. Serves as origin where replication initiates
C. DNA ligase III. Polymerises deoxynucleotides exclusively in \(5'\rightarrow 3'\) direction
D. Origin of replication IV. Dual role as substrate and source of energy

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The question requires pairing enzymes and functional elements involved in prokaryotic DNA replication with their precise operational characteristics.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Mechanisms
- DNA-dependent DNA polymerase is an efficient enzyme that catalyses polymerisation of deoxynucleotides with high fidelity strictly in the \(5'\rightarrow 3'\) direction on the newly synthesised strand.
- Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) serve dual purposes: acting as substrates for building the DNA polymer and providing high-energy phosphate bonds (through cleavage of the two terminal phosphates) to fuel the polymerisation reaction.
- DNA ligase catalyses the formation of phosphodiester bonds to covalently join discontinuously synthesised fragments (Okazaki fragments) on the lagging strand.
- Origin of replication is a definite sequence in the DNA where replication originates; without it, propagation and replication of DNA cannot occur.

Step 3: Pairing Identification
- DNA-dependent DNA polymerase associates with polymerising deoxynucleotides exclusively in \(5'\rightarrow 3'\) direction.
- Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates associate with dual role as substrate and source of energy.
- DNA ligase associates with joining discontinuously synthesised fragments.
- Origin of replication associates with serving as origin where replication initiates.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
All biochemical properties and physiological roles match the replication machinery described in the text.
Final Answer: The correct matching is DNA-dependent DNA polymerase with Polymerises deoxynucleotides exclusively in \(5'\rightarrow 3'\) direction; Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates with Dual role as substrate and source of energy; DNA ligase with Joins discontinuously synthesised fragments; and Origin of replication with Serves as origin where replication initiates.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q05 - Match eukaryotic and bacterial RNA polymerases

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Polymerase / Catalytic RNA) List-II (Transcribed Product / Activity)
A. RNA polymerase I I. Heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA)
B. RNA polymerase II II. \(28\text{S}\), \(18\text{S}\), and \(5.8\text{S}\) rRNAs
C. RNA polymerase III III. Ribozyme forming peptide bonds during translation
D. Bacterial \(23\text{S}\) rRNA IV. tRNA, \(5\text{S}\) rRNA, and snRNAs

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The problem focuses on division of labour among eukaryotic nuclear RNA polymerases and the catalytic function of bacterial ribosomal RNA.

Step 2: Relevant Principles of Transcription and Translation
- In eukaryotic nuclei, RNA polymerase I is responsible for transcribing ribosomal RNAs, namely the \(28\text{S}\), \(18\text{S}\), and \(5.8\text{S}\) rRNAs.
- RNA polymerase II transcribes the precursor of messenger RNA, known as heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).
- RNA polymerase III transcribes transfer RNA (tRNA), \(5\text{S}\) rRNA, and small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs).
- In bacteria, the \(23\text{S}\) rRNA functions as a catalytic RNA molecule (ribozyme) that catalyses the formation of peptide bonds during protein synthesis.

Step 3: Pairing Identification
- RNA polymerase I associates with \(28\text{S}\), \(18\text{S}\), and \(5.8\text{S}\) rRNAs.
- RNA polymerase II associates with heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).
- RNA polymerase III associates with tRNA, \(5\text{S}\) rRNA, and snRNAs.
- Bacterial \(23\text{S}\) rRNA associates with ribozyme forming peptide bonds during translation.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The specificity of RNA synthesis and RNA-mediated catalysis confirms that each assigned pair is biochemically exact.
Final Answer: The correct matching is RNA polymerase I with \(28\text{S}\), \(18\text{S}\), and \(5.8\text{S}\) rRNAs; RNA polymerase II with Heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA); RNA polymerase III with tRNA, \(5\text{S}\) rRNA, and snRNAs; and Bacterial \(23\text{S}\) rRNA with Ribozyme forming peptide bonds during translation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q06 - Match RNA processing and noncoding features

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Process / Structural Region) List-II (Biochemical Definition)
A. Splicing I. Addition of methyl guanosine triphosphate to the \(5'\)-end
B. Capping II. Removal of introns and joining of exons in a defined order
C. Tailing III. Sequences present at both ends of mRNA required for efficient translation
D. Untranslated regions (UTRs) IV. Addition of 200–300 adenylate residues at the \(3'\)-end

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The task requires matching post-transcriptional modifications of eukaryotic primary transcripts (hnRNA) and untranslated structural features of mRNA with their biochemical descriptions.

Step 2: Relevant Principles and Post-transcriptional Events
- Splicing is the molecular process by which non-coding intervening sequences (introns) are excised from primary transcripts and coding sequences (exons) are joined together in a defined sequence to produce mature mRNA.
- Capping involves the covalent attachment of an unusual modified nucleotide, 7-methylguanosine triphosphate (\(\text{m}^7\text{G}_{\text{ppp}}\)), to the \(5'\)-end of the nascent hnRNA.
- Tailing (polyadenylation) consists of the template-independent enzymatic addition of 200 to 300 adenylate residues at the \(3'\)-end of the RNA.
- Untranslated regions (UTRs) are nucleotide segments present on mature mRNA before the initiation codon at the \(5'\)-end and after the stop codon at the \(3'\)-end that are essential for efficient translation.

Step 3: Pairing Identification
- Splicing associates with removal of introns and joining of exons in a defined order.
- Capping associates with addition of methyl guanosine triphosphate to the \(5'\)-end.
- Tailing associates with addition of 200–300 adenylate residues at the \(3'\)-end.
- Untranslated regions (UTRs) associate with sequences present at both ends of mRNA required for efficient translation.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Each operational definition corresponds unequivocally to its post-transcriptional or mRNA structural counterpart.
Final Answer: The correct matching is Splicing with Removal of introns and joining of exons in a defined order; Capping with Addition of methyl guanosine triphosphate to the \(5'\)-end; Tailing with Addition of 200–300 adenylate residues at the \(3'\)-end; and Untranslated regions (UTRs) with Sequences present at both ends of mRNA required for efficient translation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q08 - Match codons and genetic code properties

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Codon / Characteristic) List-II (Feature / Assigned Meaning)
A. AUG I. Polynucleotide phosphorylase used for template-independent RNA synthesis
B. UAA, UAG, UGA II. Codes specifically for Phenylalanine
C. UUU III. Dual functions: codes for Methionine and acts as initiator codon
D. Severo Ochoa enzyme IV. Stop or termination codons that do not code for any amino acid

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The problem requires matching specific triplet codons and enzymatic tools of genetic code elucidation with their biochemical attributes.

Step 2: Relevant Principles of the Genetic Code
- The triplet codon AUG possesses dual functions: it encodes the amino acid methionine and serves as the initiator codon for translation.
- The three codons UAA, UAG, and UGA do not code for any amino acids; they lack corresponding aminoacyl-tRNAs and therefore function as stop or termination codons.
- The homopolymer codon UUU was the first triplet deciphered and codes unambiguously for phenylalanine.
- Severo Ochoa enzyme is polynucleotide phosphorylase, which was instrumental in deciphering the code because it polymerises RNA with defined sequences in a template-independent manner.

Step 3: Pairing Identification
- AUG associates with dual functions: codes for Methionine and acts as initiator codon.
- UAA, UAG, UGA associate with stop or termination codons that do not code for any amino acid.
- UUU associates with coding specifically for Phenylalanine.
- Severo Ochoa enzyme associates with polynucleotide phosphorylase used for template-independent RNA synthesis.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Each codon assignment and biochemical definition corresponds precisely to the genetic code rules.
Final Answer: The correct matching is AUG with Dual functions: codes for Methionine and acts as initiator codon; UAA, UAG, UGA with Stop or termination codons that do not code for any amino acid; UUU with Codes specifically for Phenylalanine; and Severo Ochoa enzyme with Polynucleotide phosphorylase used for template-independent RNA synthesis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q10 - Match DNA fingerprinting methods and terms

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Method / Component) List-II (Role in DNA Profiling)
A. Alec Jeffreys I. Cleaves high molecular weight genomic DNA at specific sites
B. Restriction endonucleases II. Mini-satellite tandem repeats ranging from \(0.1\text{ to }20\text{ kb}\) used as probes
C. Agarose gel electrophoresis III. Developed the original DNA fingerprinting technique
D. Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR) IV. Separates cut DNA fragments according to size

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The task requires matching techniques, scientists, and molecular markers integral to DNA fingerprinting with their functional definitions.

Step 2: Relevant Principles of DNA Fingerprinting
- Sir Alec Jeffreys developed the original technique of DNA fingerprinting using satellite DNA probes displaying high polymorphism.
- Restriction endonucleases are molecular scissors that digest and cleave long genomic DNA into manageable fragments at specific recognition sequences.
- Agarose gel electrophoresis is the analytical separation technique that resolves negatively charged DNA fragments on the basis of their molecular size.
- Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR) belongs to mini-satellite DNA repeats where short sequence units are tandemly repeated, varying in size from \(0.1\text{ to }20\text{ kb}\), serving as highly polymorphic radiolabelled probes during Southern blot hybridisation.

Step 3: Pairing Identification
- Alec Jeffreys associates with developing the original DNA fingerprinting technique.
- Restriction endonucleases associate with cleaving high molecular weight genomic DNA at specific sites.
- Agarose gel electrophoresis associates with separating cut DNA fragments according to size.
- Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR) associates with mini-satellite tandem repeats ranging from \(0.1\text{ to }20\text{ kb}\) used as probes.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Each technological step matches its operational mechanism in forensic and paternity DNA analysis.
Final Answer: The correct matching is Alec Jeffreys with Developed the original DNA fingerprinting technique; Restriction endonucleases with Cleaves high molecular weight genomic DNA at specific sites; Agarose gel electrophoresis with Separates cut DNA fragments according to size; and Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR) with Mini-satellite tandem repeats ranging from \(0.1\text{ to }20\text{ kb}\) used as probes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q01 - Sequential steps in the Southern blot DNA fingerprinting technique

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following major laboratory steps of the DNA fingerprinting technique originally developed by Alec Jeffreys in the correct chronological sequence:

  1. Hybridisation of DNA fragments using a radiolabelled VNTR probe
  2. Digestion of isolated genomic DNA by restriction endonucleases
  3. Detection of hybridised radioactive bands by autoradiography
  4. Separation of cleaved DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis
  5. Transferring (blotting) of separated DNA fragments to synthetic membranes such as nitrocellulose or nylon

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Context
The task requires organizing the sequential experimental stages of DNA fingerprinting (Southern blot hybridisation using Variable Number of Tandem Repeats) as originally established by Alec Jeffreys.

Step 2: Principles and Logical Workflow
The protocol proceeds in a defined logical and biochemical sequence:
1. High molecular weight genomic DNA is first extracted and isolated from cellular samples.
2. The isolated DNA is enzymatically cleaved at specific recognition sequences using restriction endonucleases to generate fragments of varying sizes.
3. These restriction fragments are loaded onto a gel matrix and separated according to their molecular size via agarose gel electrophoresis under an electric field.
4. The resolved double-stranded fragments are denatured and transferred (blotted) from the fragile agarose gel onto a durable synthetic membrane, such as nitrocellulose or nylon.
5. The membrane is incubated with single-stranded, radiolabelled Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR) mini-satellite probes that hybridise specifically to complementary polymorphic repeat sequences.
6. Unbound probe is washed away, and the hybridised bands are detected and visualised by exposing X-ray film to the membrane in autoradiography.

Step 3: Verification of the Proper Order
Following the isolation of DNA, the necessary operational order is:
- First, restriction endonuclease digestion.
- Second, agarose gel electrophoresis to separate fragments.
- Third, southern blotting to transfer fragments onto a synthetic membrane.
- Fourth, hybridisation with the radiolabelled VNTR probe.
- Fifth, autoradiographic detection to obtain the characteristic banding pattern.

Final Answer:
The correct chronological order of the process is: Digestion of isolated genomic DNA by restriction endonucleases \(\rightarrow\) Separation of cleaved DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis \(\rightarrow\) Transferring (blotting) of separated DNA fragments to synthetic membranes \(\rightarrow\) Hybridisation of DNA fragments using a radiolabelled VNTR probe \(\rightarrow\) Detection of hybridised radioactive bands by autoradiography.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MOLECULAR_BASIS_OF_INHERITANCE_MCQ_Q02 - Logical sequence of events during translation in prokaryotes

questiontext.text:
The following events occur during the process of translation (protein synthesis) in a prokaryotic cell:

  1. Binding of a release factor to the termination codon at the A-site, releasing the complete polypeptide
  2. Activation of amino acids in the presence of ATP and linking to their cognate tRNA (aminoacylation)
  3. Association of the small subunit of the ribosome with mRNA and positioning at the start codon (AUG)
  4. Movement of the ribosome from codon to codon along the mRNA with peptide bond formation catalysed by \(23\text{S}\) rRNA
  5. Recognition of the initiator codon by the initiator tRNA carrying activated methionine

Select the option that represents the correct sequential order of these translational events from start to finish:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Biochemical Context
The problem addresses the molecular mechanism of translation in prokaryotes, spanning amino acid activation, translation initiation, elongation, and termination.

Step 2: Principles Governing Translation
- Energetic activation: Peptide bond synthesis requires free energy. In the first phase, amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and esterified to their cognate tRNA, a prerequisite termed aminoacylation or charging of tRNA.
- Initiation: In its inactive state, the ribosome exists as separated large and small subunits. When the small ribosomal subunit encounters an mRNA, translation begins. It binds near the start codon (AUG).
- Initiator complex formation: The initiation codon (AUG) is specifically recognized by the initiator tRNA bearing formyl-methionine, completing the initiation complex alongside the assembly of the large subunit.
- Elongation: The ribosome translocates from codon to codon along the mRNA in the \(5'\rightarrow 3'\) direction. Successive charged tRNAs enter, pairing anticodons with codons. In bacteria, the \(23\text{S}\) rRNA acts as a ribozyme (peptidyl transferase) that catalyses peptide bond formation between adjacent amino acids.
- Termination: When a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) reaches the A-site, no tRNA binds to it. Instead, a protein release factor binds directly to the stop codon, terminating translation and releasing the synthesized polypeptide from the ribosome.

Step 3: Determination of the Correct Order
- Aminoacylation of tRNA must occur first before protein assembly can begin.
- Next, the small ribosomal subunit encounters and binds the mRNA at the initiation site.
- The initiator tRNA then recognizes and base-pairs with the AUG start codon.
- Elongation and peptide bond synthesis catalysed by the \(23\text{S}\) rRNA ribozyme proceed iteratively along the mRNA transcript.
- Finally, termination occurs when a release factor recognizes the stop codon and releases the polypeptide.

Final Answer:
The correct chronological order is: Activation of amino acids in the presence of ATP and linking to their cognate tRNA \(\rightarrow\) Association of the small subunit of the ribosome with mRNA at the start codon \(\rightarrow\) Recognition of the initiator codon by the initiator tRNA \(\rightarrow\) Movement of the ribosome along the mRNA with peptide bond formation catalysed by \(23\text{S}\) rRNA \(\rightarrow\) Binding of a release factor to the termination codon, releasing the complete polypeptide.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q01 - Number of nucleotides in bacteriophage phi cross 174

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The length of DNA is defined by the number of nucleotides or base pairs present in it, which serves as a characteristic feature of an organism.

Step 2: Analysis of the Genome
Bacteriophage \(\phi \times 174\) possesses a single-stranded circular DNA genome containing 5386 nucleotides.

Step 3: Comparison with Related Organisms
By contrast, bacteriophage lambda contains 48502 base pairs, Escherichia coli contains \(4.6 \times 10^6\) base pairs, and the human haploid genome comprises \(3.3 \times 10^9\) base pairs.

The exact nucleotide count of bacteriophage \(\phi \times 174\) is 5386 nucleotides.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is 5386 nucleotides.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q02 - Nitrogenous base linkage to pentose sugar in nucleosides

questiontext.text: In the chemical structure of a polynucleotide chain, a nitrogenous base is covalently linked to the pentose sugar via which specific linkage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A nucleoside is formed by the union of a nitrogenous base with a pentose sugar molecule.

Step 2: Identification of the Chemical Linkage
The nitrogenous base is attached to the hydroxyl group of the 1'-carbon of the pentose sugar through an N-glycosidic linkage.

Step 3: Verification of Other Bond Types
A phosphoester linkage connects the 5'-hydroxyl of the nucleoside to a phosphate group, while 3'-5' phosphodiester linkages join adjacent nucleotides in the backbone.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The linkage joining a nitrogenous base to the 1'-carbon of the pentose sugar is an N-glycosidic linkage.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is N-glycosidic linkage at the 1'-carbon of the pentose sugar.

Histone proteins are rich in the basic amino acid residues lysine and arginine.

Both lysine and arginine residues carry positive charges in their side chains, enabling histones to bind tightly to negatively charged DNA molecules.

The basic amino acid residues abundant in histones are lysine and arginine.

Friedrich Miescher isolated an acidic, phosphorus-rich substance from the nuclei of pus cells and designated it as 'Nuclein'.

The term nucleic acid was applied later, and Watson and Crick elucidated the double helical structure of DNA in 1953.

The substance originally isolated and named by Friedrich Miescher was nuclein.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q05 - Virulent strain characteristics in Griffith transformation experiment

The S strain bacteria synthesize a smooth mucous (polysaccharide) coat, yielding smooth shiny colonies, and are virulent, killing infected mice.

Step 3: Comparison with the R Strain
The R strain lacks this polysaccharide coat, forms rough colonies, and is avirulent, allowing infected mice to survive.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The virulent strain responsible for fatal pneumonia is the S strain possessing a mucous polysaccharide coat.

generalfeedback.text:

In the Meselson and Stahl experiment, isotopes of nitrogen were utilized to differentially label parental and newly synthesized DNA strands.

Step 2: Physical Properties of the Isotope
The isotope \(^{15}\text{N}\) is a stable, heavy isotope of nitrogen; it is non-radioactive.

Step 3: Separation Technique
Molecules containing \(^{15}\text{N}\) are resolved from normal \(^{14}\text{N}\)-containing molecules strictly based on differences in density using cesium chloride (CsCl) density gradient centrifugation.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The isotope \(^{15}\text{N}\) is a heavy, non-radioactive isotope separated based on density differences.

Final Answer:

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q07 - Initiation factor associating with bacterial RNA polymerase

questiontext.text: In bacterial transcription, the core RNA polymerase enzyme associates transiently with which factor to initiate transcription specifically at the promoter?

Bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is capable of catalyzing the elongation phase of transcription on its own but requires regulatory factors for initiation and termination.

The RNA polymerase associates transiently with the initiation-factor sigma (\(\sigma\)) to recognize the promoter region and initiate transcription.

Step 3: Role of Termination Factor
The termination-factor rho (\(\rho\)) associates transiently with RNA polymerase at the terminator region to stop transcription and release the nascent RNA.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The factor responsible for conferring initiation specificity to bacterial RNA polymerase is the sigma factor.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Sigma (\(\sigma\)) factor.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q10 - Polymorphic probe utilized in Alec Jeffreys technique

questiontext.text: The classical technique of DNA fingerprinting was initially developed by Alec Jeffreys using which polymorphic DNA sequence as a hybridization probe?

generalfeedback.text:

DNA fingerprinting identifies variations in specific DNA regions where short stretches of base sequences are repeated tandemly.

Step 2: Historical Development by Jeffreys
Alec Jeffreys utilized a satellite DNA showing high degrees of polymorphism, known as Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR), as a radiolabeled probe.

Therefore, the correct answer is Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q11 - Percentage of adenine calculated from cytosine content

questiontext.text: A sample of double-stranded DNA is analyzed and found to contain 20% cytosine. According to Chargaff's rules of base equivalence, what is the percentage of adenine present in this DNA molecule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The DNA is double-stranded. Cytosine content (\(\text{C}\)) is given as 20%.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard Watson-Crick base pairing applies: adenine pairs exclusively with thymine, and guanine pairs exclusively with cytosine.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Erwin Chargaff's rules for double-stranded DNA:
\(\text{A} = \text{T}\) and \(\text{G} = \text{C}\)
The sum of all four bases equals 100%:
\(\text{A} + \text{T} + \text{G} + \text{C} = 100\%\)

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(\text{G} = \text{C}\), and \(\text{C} = 20\%\), we have:
\(\text{G} = 20\%\)
Therefore, the total \(\text{G} + \text{C}\) content is:
\(20\% + 20\% = 40\%\)
The remaining percentage represents \(\text{A} + \text{T}\):
\(\text{A} + \text{T} = 100\% - 40\% = 60\%\)
Because \(\text{A} = \text{T}\), the percentage of adenine is:
\(\text{A} = \frac{60\%}{2} = 30\%\)

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check: \(30\% \text{ (A)} + 30\% \text{ (T)} + 20\% \text{ (G)} + 20\% \text{ (C)} = 100\%\). The ratio \(\frac{\text{A}+\text{G}}{\text{T}+\text{C}} = \frac{50}{50} = 1\). Thus, the percentage of adenine is 30%.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is 30%.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q12 - Structural basis of polynucleotide chain terminal polarity

questiontext.text: What determines the distinct 5' and 3' terminal polarities of a single polynucleotide chain in nucleic acids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A polynucleotide chain exhibits directional polarity governed by the orientation and free functional groups of its constituent pentose sugars.

Step 2: Analysis of the 5'-End
At one terminus of the polymer, the pentose sugar carries an unlinked, free phosphate moiety attached to the 5'-carbon atom, defining the 5'-end.

Step 3: Analysis of the 3'-End
At the opposite terminus, the pentose sugar bears a free hydroxyl (-OH) group linked to the 3'-carbon atom, defining the 3'-end.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The polarity of the chain is established by a free phosphate group at the 5'-carbon of the sugar at one terminus and a free hydroxyl group at the 3'-carbon of the sugar at the other terminus.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is A free phosphate moiety at the 5'-carbon of the sugar at one end and a free hydroxyl group at the 3'-carbon of the sugar at the other end.

answer.text: A free phosphate moiety at the 5'-carbon of the sugar at one end and a free hydroxyl group at the 3'-carbon of the sugar at the other end
A free hydroxyl group at the 5'-carbon of the sugar and a free phosphate moiety at the 3'-carbon of the sugar
An attached purine base at the 5'-end and an attached pyrimidine base at the 3'-end
A 3'-N-glycosidic bond at one end and a 5'-phosphoester bond at the opposite end

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q13 - Helix pitch and base pair distance parameters

questiontext.text: In the Watson and Crick double helix model of B-DNA, what are the pitch of the helix and the distance between adjacent base pairs, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
B-DNA forms a right-handed double helix with regular geometric parameters defining each helical turn.

Step 2: Evaluation of Helical Pitch
The pitch of the DNA helix is \(3.4\text{ nm}\) (where \(1\text{ nm} = 10^{-9}\text{ m}\)).

Step 3: Evaluation of Base Pair Spacing
There are roughly 10 base pairs per helical turn. Consequently, the distance separating two consecutive base pairs is approximately \(\frac{3.4\text{ nm}}{10} = 0.34\text{ nm}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The pitch of the helix is \(3.4\text{ nm}\) and the distance between consecutive base pairs is \(0.34\text{ nm}\).

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is \(3.4\text{ nm}\) and \(0.34\text{ nm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q14 - Number of nucleosomes in diploid mammalian cell

questiontext.text: Assuming that a typical nucleosome contains 200 base pairs of DNA, approximately how many nucleosome units are present in a diploid human cell containing \(6.6 \times 10^9\text{ bp}\) of DNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total length of diploid human DNA = \(6.6 \times 10^9\text{ bp}\). DNA length per nucleosome = \(200\text{ bp}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Assume uniform wrapping of genomic DNA into standard nucleosomal repeating units across the genome.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The theoretical number of nucleosomes is determined by dividing total base pairs by base pairs per nucleosome:
\[\text{Number of nucleosomes} = \frac{\text{Total base pairs}}{\text{Base pairs per nucleosome}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values:
\[\text{Number of nucleosomes} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^9}{200} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^9}{2 \times 10^2} = 3.3 \times 10^7\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Multiplying \(3.3 \times 10^7\text{ nucleosomes} \times 200\text{ bp/nucleosome} = 6.6 \times 10^9\text{ bp}\), confirming the calculation. The approximate number of nucleosomes is \(3.3 \times 10^7\).

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is \(3.3 \times 10^7\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q15 - Distinguishing characteristics of euchromatin and heterochromatin

questiontext.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes euchromatin from heterochromatin in a eukaryotic cell nucleus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chromatin in a typical nucleus exhibits regions of differential packaging density and transcriptional potential.

Step 2: Characteristics of Euchromatin
Euchromatin represents loosely packed regions of chromatin that stain lightly and correspond to transcriptionally active genetic material.

Step 3: Characteristics of Heterochromatin
Heterochromatin represents densely packed regions that stain darkly under microscopic examination and represent transcriptionally inactive chromatin.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Euchromatin is loosely packed, light-staining, and transcriptionally active, whereas heterochromatin is densely packed, dark-staining, and transcriptionally inactive.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Euchromatin is loosely packed, stains lightly, and is transcriptionally active, whereas heterochromatin is densely packed, stains dark, and is inactive.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q16 - Effect of digestive enzymes on bacterial transformation

questiontext.text: In the experiments by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty to biochemically characterize the transforming principle, what was the effect of treating purified heat-killed S-cell extracts with proteases, RNases, and DNase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Specific hydrolytic enzymes selectively degrade individual macromolecular classes to determine which biomolecule is necessary and sufficient for biological transformation.

Step 2: Effects of Proteases and RNases
Treatment of the transforming extract with protein-digesting enzymes (proteases) or RNA-digesting enzymes (RNases) did not affect transformation, proving that neither protein nor RNA was the transforming agent.

Step 3: Effect of DNase
Digestion of the extract with deoxyribonuclease (DNase) completely abolished the ability to transform live R cells into virulent S cells.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Proteases and RNases did not inhibit transformation, whereas DNase completely inhibited transformation, establishing that DNA is the transforming substance.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Proteases and RNases did not affect transformation, whereas DNase completely inhibited transformation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q17 - Localization of radioactive signals in Hershey Chase

questiontext.text: In the Hershey-Chase experiment, when E. coli bacteria were infected with bacteriophages labeled with \(^{35}\text{S}\) or \(^{32}\text{P}\), where was radioactivity primarily detected after blending and centrifugation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Centrifugation separates heavier bacterial cells into a pellet at the bottom of the tube, while lighter viral protein coats remain suspended in the supernatant fluid.

Step 2: Tracking the \(^{35}\text{S}\) Label
Sulfur is present in proteins but absent in DNA. Bacteriophages grown in \(^{35}\text{S}\) had radioactive protein coats, and following agitation and centrifugation, radioactivity was detected in the supernatant rather than the bacterial pellet.

Step 3: Tracking the \(^{32}\text{P}\) Label
Phosphorus is present in DNA but absent in proteins. Phages grown in \(^{32}\text{P}\) injected their radioactive DNA into the bacteria, resulting in radioactivity being detected in the bacterial pellet.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
\(^{35}\text{S}\) was recovered in the supernatant fluid, whereas \(^{32}\text{P}\) was localized within the bacterial pellet.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is \(^{35}\text{S}\) was detected in the supernatant, whereas \(^{32}\text{P}\) was detected in the bacterial cells (pellet).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q18 - Chemical factors providing enhanced stability to DNA

questiontext.text: Which chemical and structural differences make DNA a more stable and preferred genetic material compared to RNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Genetic material must be structurally and chemically stable so as not to change haphazardly across physiological states or life stages.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Pentose Sugar
In RNA, every nucleotide residue has a reactive 2'-hydroxyl (-OH) group in its ribose sugar, making RNA labile, reactive, and easily degradable. DNA lacks this 2'-OH group (having deoxyribose).

Step 3: Evaluation of Nitrogenous Bases
DNA contains thymine (5-methyl uracil) instead of uracil, which confers additional chemical stability and resistance to deamination.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The absence of a reactive 2'-OH group on the pentose sugar and the presence of thymine instead of uracil make DNA structurally and chemically more stable than RNA.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Absence of a 2'-hydroxyl group in deoxyribose and the presence of thymine instead of uracil.

answer.text: Absence of a 2'-hydroxyl group in deoxyribose and the presence of thymine instead of uracil

Absence of hydrogen bonding between purines and pyrimidines

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q19 - Proportion of hybrid to light DNA molecules

questiontext.text: In a Meselson-Stahl experiment, E. coli cells fully adapted to \(^{15}\text{N}\) medium were transferred to \(^{14}\text{N}\) medium and grown for 80 minutes. Given that the generation time of E. coli is 20 minutes, what is the proportion of hybrid (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)) to light (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)) DNA molecules at 80 minutes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial DNA has both strands labeled with \(^{15}\text{N}\) (1 heavy molecule = 2 \(^{15}\text{N}\) strands). Generation time = 20 minutes. Total time = 80 minutes.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
DNA replication is semiconservative. Each original strand acts as a template for a new \(^{14}\text{N}\) strand.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Number of generations \(n = \frac{\text{Total time}}{\text{Generation time}} = \frac{80}{20} = 4\). Total DNA molecules formed \(= 2^n = 2^4 = 16\). The two original \(^{15}\text{N}\) strands persist, so exactly 2 hybrid molecules are formed regardless of generation count for \(n \ge 1\). The remaining molecules are light (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Total molecules = 16.
Number of hybrid molecules (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)) = 2.
Number of light molecules (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)) = \(16 - 2 = 14\).
Ratio of hybrid to light DNA = \(2 : 14 = 1 : 7\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check: 2 hybrid + 14 light = 16 total duplexes. The proportion of hybrid to light DNA molecules is 1 : 7.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is 1 : 7 (or 2 hybrid to 14 light molecules).

answer.text: 1 : 1 (or equal amounts of hybrid and light molecules)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q20 - Experimental demonstration of semiconservative replication in plants

questiontext.text: Semiconservative replication of DNA in eukaryotic chromosomes was experimentally proven in 1958 by Taylor and colleagues using which biological material and technique?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Taylor and coworkers verified that eukaryotic chromosome replication conforms to the semiconservative distribution model postulated by Watson and Crick.

Step 2: Biological Specimen
The experiment was conducted on the dividing root tip cells of the broad bean plant, Vicia faba.

Step 3: Labeling and Detection Method
They used radioactive thymidine to specifically label replicating DNA and detected the distribution of radioactivity in metaphase chromosomes via autoradiography.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The experiment was performed on Vicia faba using radioactive thymidine.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Radioactive thymidine on Vicia faba.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q21 - Dual functional roles of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates

questiontext.text: During DNA replication, what dual purposes are served by deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA polymerisation is a high-speed, energetically demanding anabolic biochemical reaction.

Step 2: Substrate Function
Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dATP, dGTP, dCTP, dTTP) provide the monomeric building blocks (deoxynucleotides) that are joined to form the new polynucleotide strand.

Step 3: Energetic Function
The two terminal phosphate groups in dNTPs are connected by high-energy phosphoanhydride bonds (analogous to ATP). Hydrolysis of pyrophosphate releases free energy that powers the polymerisation reaction.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates act both as monomeric substrates and as energy donors for the polymerisation reaction.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Acting as substrates and providing energy for polymerisation via high-energy terminal phosphates.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q22 - Directionality and strand synthesis at replication fork

questiontext.text: Because DNA-dependent DNA polymerase can catalyze polymerisation only in the 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3' direction, how is DNA synthesized on the two antiparallel template strands at a replication fork?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The replication fork exposes two template strands with opposite polarities: 3' \(\rightarrow\) 5' and 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3'.

Step 2: Synthesis on the 3' \(\rightarrow\) 5' Template
On the template strand with polarity 3' \(\rightarrow\) 5', DNA polymerase synthesizes a complementary strand continuously in the 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3' direction toward the advancing fork.

Step 3: Synthesis on the 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3' Template
On the template strand with polarity 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3', polymerisation occurs discontinuously away from the fork in short fragments (5' \(\rightarrow\) 3'), which are later joined by DNA ligase.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Replication is continuous on the template strand with polarity 3' \(\rightarrow\) 5' and discontinuous on the template strand with polarity 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3'.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Continuous on the 3' \(\rightarrow\) 5' template and discontinuous on the 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3' template.

answer.text: Continuous on the 3' \(\rightarrow\) 5' template and discontinuous on the 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3' template

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q23 - Reference strand for defining transcription unit orientation

questiontext.text: By scientific convention, all reference points used to define structural elements of a transcription unit (such as the promoter and terminator) are established relative to which strand?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a transcription unit, DNA contains two strands with opposite polarity: the template strand (3' \(\rightarrow\) 5') and the coding strand (5' \(\rightarrow\) 3').

Step 2: Defining the Coding Strand
The strand with 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3' polarity has a sequence identical to the transcribed RNA (except with thymine instead of uracil). Although it is displaced and does not serve as a template, it is designated as the coding strand.

Step 3: Convention of Reference
All spatial descriptions—such as locating the promoter upstream at the 5'-end and the terminator downstream at the 3'-end—are made exclusively with respect to the coding strand.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
All reference points in a transcription unit are defined with respect to the coding strand.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is The coding strand.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q24 - Architecture of split genes in eukaryotic genomes

questiontext.text: In eukaryotic genomes, what structural feature defines a 'split gene' in a monocistronic transcription unit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Unlike prokaryotic structural genes, eukaryotic structural genes contain interrupted coding sequences.

Step 2: Definition of Exons and Introns
The expressed coding sequences that appear in mature, functional messenger RNA are called exons. These exons are interrupted by intervening, non-coding sequences termed introns.

Step 3: Fate of Introns
Introns are transcribed into precursor hnRNA but are removed by RNA splicing and do not appear in processed mRNA.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
A split gene is characterized by expressed coding sequences (exons) that are interrupted by intervening non-coding sequences (introns).

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Coding sequences (exons) that appear in mature RNA are interrupted by intervening non-coding sequences (introns).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q25 - Specific RNA polymerase transcribing major ribosomal RNAs

questiontext.text: In the nucleus of eukaryotic cells, which distinct RNA polymerase is responsible for transcribing the 28S, 18S, and 5.8S ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Eukaryotes possess a distinct division of labor involving three nuclear DNA-dependent RNA polymerases.

Step 2: Specificity of RNA Polymerase I
RNA polymerase I is localized in the nucleolus and transcribes the large ribosomal RNA precursor that yields 28S, 18S, and 5.8S rRNAs.

Step 3: Specificity of Other Polymerases
RNA polymerase II synthesizes hnRNA (the precursor to mRNA), while RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA, and small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The transcription of 28S, 18S, and 5.8S rRNAs is catalyzed by RNA polymerase I.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is RNA polymerase I.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q26 - Capping and tailing modifications in eukaryotic hnRNA

questiontext.text: During the processing of eukaryotic heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA) into mature mRNA, what chemical modifications occur during capping and tailing?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Primary eukaryotic transcripts (hnRNA) undergo enzyme-mediated post-transcriptional modifications at both termini to become stable, translatable mRNAs.

Step 2: Mechanism of Capping
In capping, an unusual nucleotide, methyl guanosine triphosphate (\(^\text{m}\text{G}_{\text{ppp}}\)), is added to the 5'-end of the hnRNA.

Step 3: Mechanism of Tailing
In tailing (polyadenylation), approximately 200 to 300 adenylate residues are added to the 3'-end in a template-independent manner.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Capping involves addition of methyl guanosine triphosphate at the 5'-end, and tailing involves addition of 200-300 adenylate residues at the 3'-end.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Addition of methyl guanosine triphosphate to the 5'-end and 200-300 adenylate residues to the 3'-end.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q27 - Definition and biological meaning of code degeneracy

questiontext.text: What does the term 'degeneracy' mean when describing the properties of the genetic code?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The triplet genetic code features 64 total codons, 61 of which code for the 20 standard amino acids.

Step 2: Defining Degeneracy
Because the number of coding triplets (61) exceeds the number of amino acids (20), most amino acids are specified by more than one distinct triplet codon.

Step 3: Contrast with Unambiguity
An unambiguous code means that one particular codon specifies only one amino acid. Degeneracy means that one amino acid can be specified by multiple distinct codons.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Degeneracy signifies that a particular amino acid is coded by more than one codon.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Some amino acids are coded by more than one triplet codon.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q28 - Specific amino acid substitution in sickle cell

questiontext.text: The classical point mutation that causes sickle cell anemia involves a single base pair change in the gene encoding the \(\beta\)-globin chain, resulting in which amino acid substitution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A point mutation alters a single base pair within a structural gene, which may change a single codon and consequently substitute a single amino acid in a polypeptide.

Step 2: Identification of Mutation in Sickle Cell Anemia
In the gene for the human \(\beta\)-globin chain of hemoglobin, a transversion mutation alters the codon from GAG to GUG.

Step 3: Amino Acid Change
This mutation leads to the replacement of the acidic amino acid residue glutamate (glutamic acid) with the non-polar amino acid valine at the sixth position.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The point mutation results in the substitution of glutamate by valine.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Substitution of glutamate by valine.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q29 - Three dimensional tertiary conformation of transfer RNA

questiontext.text: While the secondary structure of transfer RNA (tRNA) resembles a clover leaf, its actual three-dimensional compact tertiary conformation appears as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transfer RNA molecules fold from a primary nucleotide sequence into a secondary base-paired stem-loop structure, which further folds into a functional tertiary shape.

Step 2: Secondary vs Tertiary Conformation
The secondary structure of tRNA when flattened into two dimensions resembles a clover leaf, displaying an acceptor arm, D-loop, anticodon loop, and T\(\psi\)C loop.

Step 3: Actual Spatial Configuration
Under physical examination (such as X-ray crystallography), the actual tertiary structure is a compact, folded molecule that resembles an inverted L.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The actual three-dimensional structure of tRNA is an inverted L.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is An inverted L.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q30 - Biochemical steps involved in charging transfer RNA

questiontext.text: In the initial preparatory phase of translation, what occurs during the process known as aminoacylation or charging of tRNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Peptide bond formation is an endergonic process requiring input of energy; thus, amino acids must be activated before ribosomal polymerization.

Step 2: Activation of Amino Acid
In the first step, amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP to form an aminoacyl-AMP enzyme complex.

Step 3: Covalent Attachment to Cognate tRNA
The activated amino acid is subsequently transferred to the 3'-acceptor stem of its cognate tRNA molecule, yielding a charged aminoacyl-tRNA.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Charging of tRNA involves activation of the amino acid in the presence of ATP and linking it to its cognate tRNA.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q31 - Ribosomal RNA acting as bacterial peptidyl transferase

questiontext.text: In bacterial translation, which ribosomal RNA component functions as a ribozyme to catalyze peptide bond formation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The ribosome functions both as a structural platform and as an enzyme (peptidyl transferase) during polypeptide synthesis.

Step 2: Catalytic Component in Bacteria
In prokaryotes, the catalytic activity that forms peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids is mediated not by a protein enzyme, but by the 23S rRNA present in the large (50S) ribosomal subunit.

Step 3: Ribozyme Classification
Because an RNA molecule performs this enzymatic catalysis, it is classified as a ribozyme.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The bacterial ribozyme catalyzing peptide bond synthesis is 23S rRNA.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is 23S rRNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q32 - Origin of i gene and repressor synthesis

questiontext.text: In the lac operon of Escherichia coli, what does the letter 'i' in the i gene signify, and what is the expression pattern of this gene?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The i gene serves as the regulatory gene controlling the transcriptional state of the lac operon structural genes.

Step 2: Derivation of the Letter 'i'
The letter 'i' does not stand for inducer; rather, it is derived from the word 'inhibitor'.

The i gene encodes the lac repressor protein and is expressed constitutively (all the time at a constant basal rate), independent of whether lactose is present or absent.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The term 'i' is derived from inhibitor, and its product (the repressor) is synthesized constitutively.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is It is derived from the word 'inhibitor', and it encodes the repressor protein which is synthesized constitutively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q33 - Strategy identifying genes expressed strictly as RNA

questiontext.text: During the Human Genome Project, the methodological approach that focused on identifying and sequencing only those genes that are expressed as RNA was known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Human Genome Project employed two principal sequencing methodologies: Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs) and Sequence Annotation.

Step 2: Methodology of ESTs
The EST approach focused exclusively on identifying all the genes that are actively transcribed into RNA molecules within cells.

Step 3: Contrast with Sequence Annotation
Sequence Annotation was the blind whole-genome approach of sequencing both coding and non-coding regions and subsequently assigning functions to specific sequences.

The methodology identifying all genes expressed as RNA is Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs).

Therefore, the correct answer is Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q34 - Chromosomes with maximum and minimum gene counts

The Y chromosome contains the fewest annotated genes, with a total of only 231 genes.

Chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and the Y chromosome has the fewest genes (231).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q35 - Sequence of transcribed RNA from specific template

questiontext.text: If the sequence of the template strand in a transcription unit is \(3'\text{-ATGCATGCATGCATGCATGCATGC-}5'\), what will be the base sequence of the newly synthesized RNA transcript?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The DNA template strand sequence is \(3'\text{-ATGCATGCATGCATGCATGCATGC-}5'\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA antiparallel to the template strand, proceeding in the 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3' direction. In RNA, uracil (U) replaces thymine (T) as the base complementary to adenine (A).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Complementary base-pairing rules during transcription dictate:
DNA 3'-A pairs with RNA 5'-U
DNA 3'-T pairs with RNA 5'-A
DNA 3'-G pairs with RNA 5'-C
DNA 3'-C pairs with RNA 5'-G

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Taking the template from 3' to 5':
3'-A \(\rightarrow\) 5'-U
3'-T \(\rightarrow\) 5'-A
3'-G \(\rightarrow\) 5'-C
3'-C \(\rightarrow\) 5'-G
Repeating this 4-base motif across the 24 nucleotides yields:
\(5'\text{-UACGUACGUACGUACGUACGUACG-}3'\).
Alternatively, the RNA sequence matches the coding strand (\(5'\text{-TACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACG-}3'\)) with T replaced by U.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The synthesized RNA has 5' to 3' polarity and complementary base composition to the 3' to 5' template strand. Thus, the sequence is \(5'\text{-UACGUACGUACGUACGUACGUACG-}3'\).

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is \(5'\text{-UACGUACGUACGUACGUACGUACG-}3'\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q36 - Average polymerisation rate of bacterial DNA polymerase

questiontext.text: Escherichia coli possesses a genome of \(4.6 \times 10^6\text{ bp}\) and completes replication in approximately 18 minutes. What is the approximate average rate of polymerisation exhibited by its DNA-dependent DNA polymerase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Genome length of E. coli = \(4.6 \times 10^6\text{ base pairs}\). Total duration of replication = \(18\text{ minutes}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Convert time from minutes to seconds:
\(18\text{ minutes} = 18 \times 60\text{ seconds} = 1080\text{ seconds}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The average rate of polymerisation is defined as:
\[\text{Rate of polymerisation} = \frac{\text{Total base pairs replicated}}{\text{Time in seconds}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the rate:
\[\text{Rate} = \frac{4.6 \times 10^6\text{ bp}}{1080\text{ s}} \approx 4259\text{ bp/second bidirectional}\]
Considering replication in living cells, the average polymerisation rate is approximately 2000 base pairs per second per replicating fork, as established in standard physiological assessments.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At approximately 2000 bp/s, in 1000 seconds the enzyme polymerises \(2 \times 10^6\text{ bp}\), which accounts for the replication fork dynamics over 18 minutes. The approximate rate is 2000 bp per second.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is Approximately 2000 base pairs per second.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q37 - Percentage distribution of DNA densities generation two

questiontext.text: In Meselson and Stahl's experiment, E. coli cultured in \(^{15}\text{N}\) medium was shifted to \(^{14}\text{N}\) medium. After two generations of growth (40 minutes), what was the percentage composition of intermediate (hybrid) density DNA and light density DNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Original culture contains heavy DNA (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)). Growth time in \(^{14}\text{N}\) medium = 40 minutes. Division time = 20 minutes.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
DNA replication is semiconservative. Generation 1 occurs at 20 minutes; Generation 2 occurs at 40 minutes.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
At Generation 0 (0 min): 100% heavy DNA (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)).
At Generation 1 (20 min): 100% hybrid DNA (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)).
At Generation 2 (40 min): Each hybrid duplex produces one hybrid and one light duplex.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Starting with 1 heavy duplex (2 heavy strands):
Generation 1 produces 2 hybrid duplexes (2 \(^{15}\text{N}\) strands, 2 \(^{14}\text{N}\) strands).
Generation 2 produces 4 duplexes total:
- 2 duplexes contain one \(^{15}\text{N}\) strand and one \(^{14}\text{N}\) strand (hybrid density).
- 2 duplexes contain two \(^{14}\text{N}\) strands (light density).
Proportions: \(\frac{2}{4} = 50\%\) hybrid DNA and \(\frac{2}{4} = 50\%\) light DNA.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The total sums to \(50\% + 50\% = 100\%\). Thus, Generation II DNA is composed of equal amounts (50% each) of hybrid and light density DNA.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is 50% hybrid density and 50% light density.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q38 - Requirement of basal expression in lac operon

questiontext.text: Why must a low, basal level of expression of the lac operon be continuously maintained in an E. coli cell, even when lactose is absent from the growth medium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Induction of the lac operon requires the physical entry of lactose (or allolactose) into the bacterial cytoplasm to bind and inactivate the lac repressor.

Step 2: Role of Lactose Permease
Lactose cannot freely diffuse across the bacterial plasma membrane in sufficient quantities; its transport depends upon the transmembrane transporter permease, which is encoded by structural gene y.

Step 3: Consequences of Zero Basal Expression
If the operon were completely repressed with zero expression, no permease would be present on the cell membrane, preventing lactose from entering the cell and rendering induction impossible.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
A basal level of expression is essential to produce sufficient permease molecules to transport lactose into the cell to initiate operon induction.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is A basal level of permease is required on the membrane to transport lactose into the cell so that induction can occur.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q39 - Impact of triplet base mutations on reading frame

questiontext.text: In a protein-coding sequence, how does the insertion or deletion of three (or a multiple of three) consecutive bases differ fundamentally in its consequence from the insertion or deletion of one or two bases?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The genetic code is read as contiguous, non-overlapping triplets without punctuations.

Step 2: Insertion or Deletion of 1 or 2 Bases
Adding or removing one or two nucleotides alters the triplet grouping of every codon downstream from that site, resulting in a frameshift mutation that completely alters the downstream amino acid sequence.

Step 3: Insertion or Deletion of 3 Bases
Adding or removing three nucleotides (or multiples thereof) adds or deletes one (or multiple) codons corresponding to whole amino acid residues, leaving the downstream reading frame completely unaltered.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Insertion or deletion of three bases adds or removes whole amino acids while preserving the downstream reading frame, unlike frameshift mutations.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is It results in the insertion or deletion of one or more amino acids while leaving the reading frame unaltered from that point onwards.

answer.text: It results in the insertion or deletion of one or more amino acids while leaving the reading frame unaltered from that point onwards

It eliminates promoter recognition, preventing the initiation of transcription

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q40 - Localization and functional significance of untranslated regions

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the location and functional significance of untranslated regions (UTRs) in messenger RNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A translational unit in mRNA is flanked by start and stop codons, but the mature mRNA contains additional flanking sequences that do not code for amino acids.

Step 2: Localization of UTRs
Untranslated regions are present at both ends of the mRNA: at the 5'-end (upstream of the start codon AUG) and at the 3'-end (downstream of the stop codon).

Step 3: Functional Importance
Although UTRs are not translated into polypeptides, they are required for efficient translation, ribosomal recognition, and mRNA stability.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
UTRs are located at both the 5'-end (before start codon) and 3'-end (after stop codon) and are required for efficient translation.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is They are present at both the 5'-end (before start codon) and 3'-end (after stop codon) and are required for an efficient translation process.

They are intervening sequences spliced out in the cytoplasm before ribosomal association

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q41 - Consequences of swapping promoter and terminator positions

questiontext.text: In a hypothetical experiment, if the positions of the promoter and terminator sequences flanking a structural gene in a transcription unit were swapped, what would be the consequence?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a transcription unit, the promoter is located towards the 5'-end and the terminator towards the 3'-end of the coding strand. RNA polymerase binds to the promoter and polymerizes in the 5' \(\rightarrow\) 3' direction.

Step 2: Role of Promoter in Defining Strands
The presence and orientation of the promoter dictate which strand serves as the template (with 3' \(\rightarrow\) 5' polarity relative to the promoter) and which strand is the coding strand.

Step 3: Effect of Position Switching
By swapping the promoter with the terminator, the orientation is inverted. Consequently, the definition of the coding and template strands is reversed, causing the previously coding strand to act as the template strand.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Swapping the promoter and terminator reverses the definition and operational identity of the template and coding strands.

Final Answer:
Therefore, the correct answer is The definition of coding and template strands would be reversed.
